title: Manual do Mundo
author: Iberê Thenório
review: I was seven and the book still smelled like fresh paint. The experiments were written as if you were expected to do them at the kitchen table, not watch adults do them on TV. The homemade rocket chapter kept me up past midnight with a plastic bottle. This is the book that made me ask 'what happens if I mix these'.

title: How to Train Your Dragon
author: Cressida Cowell
review: Hiccup is small, bad at everything the tribe cares about, and wins anyway by being smarter than the problem needs. At nine I didn't have the words for that, but the idea stuck. The humor is drier than I noticed at the time; I only got it on a reread years later. I forgot most of the plot and kept thinking about how Hiccup gets people to change their minds.

title: Percy Jackson
subtitle: The Lightning Thief
author: Rick Riordan
review: I read the whole series in two months. Riordan's trick is that Greek mythology feels like something you already knew, so it never feels like a lesson. Annabeth is written better than Percy, and I don't think that's by accident. The betrayal at the end of the first book caught me completely off guard at ten.

title: A Ilha do Tesouro
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
review: Long John Silver is the best character because the book never settles on whether he's the villain. He saves Jim twice. He switches sides whenever it suits him, and you almost respect him for it. Stevenson set out to write an adventure and ended up writing about moral ambiguity. I read it in Portuguese and had to ask about half the nautical words, which made it feel like I was on the ship.

title: Harry Potter
subtitle: Complete Series
author: J.K. Rowling
review: The series that turned reading into a habit I couldn't stop. Books five and six do something most fantasy avoids: the world gets worse as the hero gets stronger. I cried at the end of book seven, which embarrassed me at eleven. It doesn't anymore. The lore falls apart if you push on it and I don't care, because the feelings hold.

title: O Pijama Listrado
author: John Boyne
review: The ending came sooner than I expected and I sat with the book closed for a few minutes. Boyne shows the horror through a child who doesn't understand what he's seeing, and it works better than it has any right to. I read it in one sitting on a Sunday afternoon. I remember that because I went quiet at dinner and my parents asked what was wrong.

title: Auto da Compadecida
author: Ariano Suassuna
review: João Grilo wins every fight by being the smartest person in the room and the most willing to make a fool of himself. Suassuna builds a whole theology out of Northeastern folk culture and it holds together. The trial in the third act is the funniest thing I read before fifteen. It's also sad, once you think about what João Grilo wants and what he actually gets. Nothing else in Brazilian literature is quite like it.

title: O Extraordinário
author: R.J. Palacio
review: The same events told from several points of view, and each narrator notices different things. The chapter I remember is Jack's, where he only realizes he was cruel after the fact. It made me count how many times I'd been Jack without noticing. Nobody in the book gets to be simply good or bad, which is more than I expected from a middle-grade novel. It changed something small in how I treat people.

title: Dom Casmurro
author: Machado de Assis
review: I still don't know if Capitu did it, and I think that's the point. Bentinho is an unreliable narrator who doesn't know he's unreliable, and Machado pulls it off without ever winking at the reader. The prose is very good. Four stars because the jealousy spiral gets repetitive halfway through and I caught myself skimming for the moment the evidence becomes real. It never does. I know.

title: Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas
author: Machado de Assis
review: The narrator opens by mentioning he's dead, then spends the book being wrong about himself in very precise ways. For 1881 the form is strange enough that it reads almost modern. Four stars because Brás Cubas is insufferable on purpose, and some chapters drag because of it. The chapter called 'O delírio' is worth the whole book.

title: Física - Renato Brito Vol. 1
author: Renato Brito
review: The mechanics chapter changed how I think about forces: not as things that push objects, but as constraints on motion. Renato Brito's problems have a logic to them, so solving them feels like following an argument instead of grinding. I did every exercise in this volume. It's the reason I started doing well in physics olympiads.

title: Física - Renato Brito Vol. 2
author: Renato Brito
review: Electromagnetism is where a lot of people lose the thread, and this volume builds the intuition slowly enough that I didn't. The thermodynamics part is denser and I had to reread chunks of it, which I think is fair. By the end I could look at a circuit diagram and see where the energy goes, not just what connects to what. That took a few months with this book.

title: Tópicos de Física
author: Gualter, Helou & Nicolau
review: The standard Brazilian physics textbook, and it reads like one: solid explanations, good problem sets, no surprises. I used it mostly to cross-check what I'd learned from Renato Brito, and it was good for that. The optics diagrams are cleaner than most. Four stars because it does the job without much elegance. If you're studying for vestibular, it has everything. If you want to enjoy physics, start somewhere else.

title: Duna
author: Frank Herbert
review: The ecology of Arrakis is thought through more carefully than most real political science. Herbert stacks ecology, religion, colonial economics and messianic psychology into one story and doesn't water any of it down. I read it in Portuguese at fourteen and kept stopping to work out what the Fremen were really saying to each other underneath the conversation. The ending refuses to be happy. That bothered me at first, and then I saw why it had to.

title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley
quote: Nothing is so painful to the human mind as a great and sudden change.
review: Not the monster story I expected. Victor is the real problem, and Shelley makes that clear early. The creature's speech in the middle is more self-aware than anything Victor manages. My one complaint is that the frame story with Walton slows the opening. The question the book keeps asking is what you owe to something you created knowing it would suffer. I didn't have an answer at fifteen. I still don't.

title: Fahrenheit 451
author: Ray Bradbury
quote: A book is a loaded gun in the house next door.
review: Short, dense and unsettling. Bradbury's censorship is scarier than Orwell's because it needs no dictator: people stop reading on their own, and by the time the story starts the firemen are almost redundant. Mildred's story stayed with me more than Montag's. The ending works as both hope and warning. I read it in one afternoon.

title: Brave New World
author: Aldous Huxley
review: More unsettling than 1984 because control comes from comfort, not pain. Nobody is tortured; everyone is satisfied enough that resisting feels pointless. The argument between the Savage and Mustapha Mond near the end is the real thesis of the book. Mond doesn't lie. He explains why the trade is worth it and leaves you to decide if he's wrong. I wasn't sure he was, and that bothered me.

title: Atkins Physical Chemistry
author: Peter Atkins
review: University-level physical chemistry at sixteen, because my research needed the thermodynamics. I spent most of my time in the quantum chapters, and Atkins explains molecular orbital theory well enough that the math stops feeling abstract. The electrochemistry sections assume lab experience I didn't have. Four stars because it's written to go with a course, and I was reading it alone. As a reference it's excellent. On your own, parts of it take patience.

title: The Martian
author: Andy Weir
review: Watney is almost aggressively cheerful for someone who might die of a failed potato crop, and the gap between the tone and the stakes is where the book lives. The science is mostly right and Weir shows the math, so you can follow every improvised fix. The scene where NASA works out orbital mechanics on a whiteboard and then realizes someone forgot to carry a number is the funniest thing in hard sci-fi. Engineering as a way to stay alive hit differently after I started building products.

title: Project Hail Mary
author: Andy Weir
review: Better than The Martian. The science problem is more elegant, the stakes are higher, and then Rocky shows up and the book becomes something else. Two beings with nothing in common but curiosity and necessity, building a language from scratch to solve a problem together. The ending is the right ending. Rocky is the best character in either of Weir's books.

title: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!
author: Richard Feynman
review: Not really a physics book. It's about being curious without caring how that looks. Feynman is sometimes insufferable, knows it, and leaves it in, which is more honest than most memoirs. The safecracking chapters are funny with zero physics required. The chapter where he learns to draw so he can give something to people who can't follow the equations stayed with me. The best scientists are also translators.

title: The Complete Sherlock Holmes
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
review: Over a thousand pages and the quality holds, because Holmes is a method more than a character. The short stories beat the novels; the deduction chains are tighter. Watson is the real achievement: he makes Holmes readable by being the one person who finds him impressive instead of exhausting. It took me months, and it trained a habit I still use: come up with several explanations before committing to one.

title: The Official SAT Study Guide
author: College Board
review: Nobody reads this for fun. You read it until the test stops being a test and becomes a pattern you recognize. I did eight full practice tests, timed. The math is easier than Brazilian olympiad math; the time pressure is harder. The reading questions have their own logic once you accept that every right answer is backed by exact words in the text, which sounds obvious and isn't. The discipline it took was worth more than anything it taught.

title: The Wolf of Wall Street
author: Jordan Belfort
review: Belfort tells his own disaster with too much energy for it to work as a warning, and I think he knows. The selling techniques buried in the chaos are sound. What the book shows, without meaning to, is that great sales inside a rotten system doesn't produce great outcomes, just destruction at scale. The parts where he loses control of the company he built are more interesting than the parts about getting rich. Useful if you're building something, mostly as a list of what not to do.

title: Catching the Wolf of Wall Street
author: Jordan Belfort
review: Better written than the first one in some ways, because Belfort can't dress up what's happening. The cooperation process is the interesting part: who flips first, what the FBI actually needs, how long a front holds under investigation. The moments where he starts respecting the agents chasing him are the most honest pages. Four stars because the middle third drags and some of the legal detail stops being interesting. Read it after the first one.

title: The Way of the Wolf
author: Jordan Belfort
review: The straight-line system is less about manipulation than about taking uncertainty out of a conversation for both sides. The core idea: objections are rarely about the stated objection. Accept that, and the rest follows. I use pieces of it when pitching HIBEEX. Not the scripts, but the model of what someone needs to believe before saying yes. Shorter and more practical than I expected from a sales book by someone with Belfort's reputation.

title: Made in America
author: Sam Walton
review: Walton's competitiveness never lets up, but it never reads as arrogance, because most of the book is him describing what he got wrong and who he learned it from. The chapter where he flies his own plane between stores to check prices and talk to the floor staff is a better operations manual than most business books. The humility feels real because he keeps crediting specific people for specific decisions. Still reading; I'm at the chapter on distribution.

title: Zero to One
author: Peter Thiel
review: The monopoly argument is the useful part, and Thiel states it plainly: competition eats the margin that funds innovation, so build something nobody else is building. The chapter on secrets is the one I keep coming back to. A secret is something true, that most people don't believe, and that you can act on. Building HIBEEX meant having a specific answer to that. The contrarian framing gets stretched sometimes, but the core idea earns it.
